paragraphs: He hurried to the hospital where Mitya was now lying. The day after his fate was decided, Mitya had come down with a nervous fever and been sent to the prison ward of the town hospital. But several people (Alyosha, Madame Hohlakov, Lise and others) had asked Doctor Varvinsky to help, and he had put Mitya in a separate little room instead of with the other prisoners. It was the room where Smerdyakov had lain. There was a sentry at the far end of the corridor and a grating over the window, so Varvinsky could feel easy about the favor he had shown, which was not strictly legal. But he was a kind-hearted, sympathetic young man. He knew how hard it would be for a man like Mitya to be thrown all at once among robbers and murderers, and that he had to get used to it by degrees. The doctor and the overseer, and even the police captain, allowed relatives and friends to visit without any formal permission. But only Alyosha and Grushenka had come to see Mitya. Rakitin had twice tried to force his way in, but Mitya kept begging Varvinsky not to let him in.

Alyosha found him sitting on his bed in a hospital dressing gown, somewhat feverish, with a towel soaked in vinegar and water on his head. When Alyosha came in, Mitya looked at him with a vague expression, but there was something like a shade of dread in it. Since the trial he had become terribly preoccupied. Sometimes he would be silent for half an hour at a time, seeming to ponder something heavily and painfully, oblivious of everything around him. When he roused himself from his brooding and started to talk, he always spoke abruptly and never about what he really wanted to say. Sometimes he looked at his brother with a suffering face. He seemed more at ease with Grushenka than with Alyosha. True, he hardly spoke to her at all, but the moment she came in, his whole face lit up with joy.

Alyosha sat down beside him on the bed without a word. This time Mitya was waiting for Alyosha in suspense, but he did not dare to ask him anything. He found it almost unthinkable that Katya would agree to come, and yet he felt that if she did not come, something inconceivable would happen. Alyosha understood how he felt.

“Trifon Borissovitch,” Mitya began nervously, “has pulled his whole inn to pieces, I’m told. He’s torn up the flooring, taken the planks apart, split up the whole gallery, so I hear. He’s hunting for treasure all the time—the fifteen hundred roubles the prosecutor said I’d hidden there. They say he started these tricks the minute he got home. Serves him right, the swindler! The guard here told me yesterday; he comes from there.”
“Listen,” Alyosha began. “She will come, but I don’t know when. Maybe today, maybe in a few days, I can’t say. But she will come, that’s certain.”

Mitya started and was about to say something, but stayed silent. The news had a tremendous effect on him. Clearly he badly wanted to know what had been said, but again he was afraid to ask. Anything cruel or contemptuous from Katya would have cut him like a knife at that moment.
“Among other things she said this: I must be sure to set your conscience at rest about escaping. If Ivan isn’t well by then, she will see to everything herself.”
“You’ve told me that already,” Mitya remarked musingly.
“And you repeated it to Grusha,” said Alyosha.

“Yes,” Mitya admitted. “She won’t come this morning.” He looked timidly at his brother. “She won’t come till evening. When I told her yesterday that Katya was taking steps, she said nothing, but she set her mouth. She only whispered, ‘Let her!’ She understood it was important. I didn’t dare press her further. I think she understands now that Katya doesn’t care for me anymore, but loves Ivan.”
“Does she?” broke from Alyosha.

“Maybe she doesn’t. It’s just that she’s not coming this morning,” Mitya hurried to explain again. “I asked her to do something for me. You know, Ivan is better than all of us. He ought to live, not us. He will recover.”
“Would you believe it, though Katya is alarmed about him, she hardly doubts he’ll recover,” said Alyosha.
“That means she’s convinced he will die. It’s because she’s frightened that she’s so sure he’ll get well.”
“Ivan has a strong constitution, and I, too, believe there’s every hope he’ll get well,” Alyosha said anxiously.
“Yes, he’ll get well. But she’s convinced he’ll die. She has a great deal of sorrow to bear...” A silence followed. A deep anxiety was gnawing at Mitya.
“Alyosha, I love Grusha terribly,” he said suddenly, in a shaking voice full of tears.
“They won’t let her go out there to you,” Alyosha put in at once.

“And there’s something else I wanted to tell you,” Mitya went on, his voice suddenly ringing. “If they beat me on the way or out there, I won’t put up with it. I’ll kill someone and be shot for it. And this will go on for twenty years! They talk to me rudely even now. I’ve been lying here all night, judging myself. I’m not ready! I can’t resign myself. I wanted to sing a ‘hymn’; but if a guard speaks rudely to me, I haven’t the strength to bear it. For Grusha I’d bear anything ... anything except blows.... But she won’t be allowed to come there.”
Alyosha smiled gently.

“Listen, brother, once and for all,” he said. “This is what I think about it. And you know I wouldn’t lie to you. Listen: you’re not ready, and such a cross is not for you. What’s more, you don’t need a martyr’s cross when you’re not ready for it. If you had murdered our father, it would grieve me to see you reject your punishment. But you’re innocent, and such a cross is too much for you. You wanted to make yourself a different man through suffering. I say only this: remember that other man always, all your life and wherever you go, and that will be enough for you. By refusing that great cross, you’ll only feel an even greater duty all your life, and that constant feeling may do more to make you a new man than going there would. Because there you wouldn’t endure it. You’d complain, and maybe in the end you’d say, ‘I’m quits.’ The lawyer was right about that. Such heavy burdens are not for everyone. For some they’re impossible. Those are my thoughts, since you want them so much. If other men had to answer for your escape, officers or soldiers, then I wouldn’t have ‘allowed’ you,” Alyosha smiled. “But they say—the superintendent of that _étape_ told Ivan himself—that if it’s well handled there won’t be any serious inquiry, and they can get off easily. Of course, bribery is dishonest even in such a case, but I can’t take it on myself to judge, because if Ivan and Katya asked me to act for you, I know I’d go and give bribes. I have to tell you the truth. So I can’t judge what you do. But let me assure you that I will never condemn you. And it would be strange if I could judge you in this. Now I think I’ve said everything.”

“But I do condemn myself!” cried Mitya. “I’ll escape, that was settled without you; could Mitya Karamazov do anything but run away? But I’ll condemn myself, and I’ll pray for my sin forever. That’s how the Jesuits talk, isn’t it? Just like us?”
“Yes.” Alyosha smiled gently.

“I love you for always telling the whole truth and never hiding anything,” cried Mitya with a joyful laugh. “So I’ve caught my Alyosha being Jesuitical. I have to kiss you for that. Now listen to the rest; I’ll open the other side of my heart to you. This is what I planned and decided. If I run away, even with money and a passport, even to America, it will cheer me to think I’m not running away for pleasure or happiness, but into another exile, as bad as Siberia, maybe. It is as bad, Alyosha, it is! I hate that America already, damn it. Even though Grusha will be with me. Just look at her; is she an American? She’s Russian, Russian to the marrow of her bones. She’ll be homesick for the mother country, and I’ll see every hour that she’s suffering for my sake, that she’s taken up that cross for me. And what harm has she done? And how will I put up with the rabble out there, though every one of them may be better than I am? I hate that America already! They may all be wonderful at machinery, damn them, but they’re not of my soul. I love Russia, Alyosha, I love the Russian God, though I’m a scoundrel myself. I’ll choke there!” he exclaimed, his eyes suddenly flashing. His voice shook with tears. “So this is what I’ve decided, Alyosha, listen,” he began again, mastering his emotion. “As soon as I get there with Grusha, we’ll set to work on the land at once, in solitude, somewhere very remote, with wild bears. There must be remote places even there. I’m told there are still Redskins there, somewhere on the edge of the horizon. So off to the country of the _Last of the Mohicans_, and there we’ll tackle the grammar right away, Grusha and I. Work and grammar—that’s how we’ll spend three years. And by then we’ll speak English like any Englishman. And as soon as we’ve learned it—good-bye to America! We’ll run back here to Russia as American citizens. Don’t worry—we wouldn’t come to this little town. We’d hide somewhere far off, in the north or the south. I’ll be changed by then, and so will she, in America. The doctors will make me some kind of wart on my face—what’s the use of their being so mechanical!—or else I’ll put out one eye, let my beard grow a yard long, and go gray, pining for Russia. I bet they won’t recognize us. And if they do, let them send us to Siberia. I don’t care. It will show it’s our fate. We’ll work on the land here, too, somewhere in the wilds, and I’ll pass as an American all my life. But we’ll die on our own soil. That’s my plan, and it won’t be changed. Do you approve?”
“Yes,” said Alyosha, not wanting to contradict him. Mitya paused a minute and then said suddenly:
“And the way they stirred it all up at the trial! Didn’t they just stir it up!”
“If they hadn’t, you’d have been convicted just the same,” said Alyosha with a sigh.
“Yes, the people here are sick of me! God bless them, but it’s hard to take,” Mitya moaned miserably. Again there was silence for a minute.
“Alyosha, don’t keep me in agony!” he suddenly exclaimed. “Tell me, is she coming now or not? Tell me! What did she say? How did she say it?”
“She said she would come, but I don’t know whether she’ll come today. It’s hard for her, you know,” Alyosha said, looking timidly at his brother.

“I should think it is hard for her! Alyosha, it’ll drive me out of my mind. Grusha keeps looking at me. She understands. My God, calm my heart: what is it I want? I want Katya! Do I even understand what I want? It’s that headstrong, evil Karamazov spirit! No, I’m not fit for suffering. I’m a scoundrel, that’s all anyone can say.”
“Here she is!” cried Alyosha.

At that moment Katya appeared in the doorway. For an instant she stood still, gazing at Mitya with a dazed look. He leapt to his feet on impulse, and a scared look came over his face. He turned pale, but at once a timid, pleading smile appeared on his lips, and with an irresistible impulse he held out both hands to Katya. Seeing this, she flew to him. She seized him by the hands and almost by force made him sit down on the bed. She sat down beside him and, still holding his hands, pressed them violently. Several times they both tried to speak but stopped short, and again they gazed at each other in silence, with a strange smile, their eyes fixed on one another. Two minutes passed like that.
“Have you forgiven me?” Mitya faltered at last, and at the same moment, turning to Alyosha, his face working with joy, he cried, “Do you hear what I’m asking? Do you hear?”

“That’s why I loved you, because you’re generous at heart!” broke from Katya. “My forgiveness is no good to you, nor yours to me; whether you forgive me or not, you’ll always be a sore spot in my heart, and I in yours—that’s how it must be....” She stopped to catch her breath. “Why have I come?” she began again in nervous haste. “To embrace your feet, to press your hands like this until it hurts—you remember how I used to squeeze them in Moscow—to tell you again that you are my god, my joy, to tell you that I love you madly,” she moaned in anguish, and suddenly pressed his hand greedily to her lips. Tears streamed from her eyes. Alyosha stood speechless and bewildered; he had never expected to see this.

“Love is over, Mitya!” Katya began again, “but the past is painfully dear to me. Know that it always will be. But now, for one minute, let what might have been come true,” she faltered with a drawn smile, looking joyfully into his face again. “You love another woman, and I love another man, and yet I will love you forever, and you will love me; do you know that? Do you hear? Love me, love me all your life!” she cried, with a quiver almost of menace in her voice.

“I will love you, and ... do you know, Katya,” Mitya began, drawing a deep breath at each word, “do you know, five days ago, that same evening, I loved you.... When you fell down and were carried out ... All my life! So it will be, it will always be so—”
So they murmured frantic words to one another, almost meaningless, perhaps not even true, but at that moment it was all true, and they both believed what they said completely.
“Katya,” Mitya cried suddenly, “do you believe I murdered him? I know you don’t believe it now, but then ... when you gave your evidence.... Surely, surely you didn’t believe it!”

“I didn’t believe it even then. I never believed it. I hated you, and for a moment I talked myself into it. While I was giving my evidence I persuaded myself and believed it, but as soon as I’d finished speaking I stopped believing it. Don’t doubt that! I’d forgotten that I came here to punish myself,” she said, with a new note in her voice, quite unlike the loving tones of a moment before.
“Woman, you carry a heavy burden,” came, as it were, involuntarily from Mitya.
“Let me go,” she whispered. “I’ll come again. I can’t bear any more now.”

She was getting up from her seat when she suddenly let out a loud scream and staggered back. Grushenka had walked into the room suddenly and silently. No one had expected her. Katya moved quickly to the door, but when she reached Grushenka she stopped abruptly, turned white as chalk, and moaned softly, almost in a whisper:
“Forgive me!”
Grushenka stared at her and, pausing for an instant, answered in a vindictive, venomous voice:
“We’re full of hatred, my girl, you and I! We’re both full of hatred! As if we could forgive each other! Save him, and I’ll worship you all my life.”
“You won’t forgive her!” cried Mitya, with frantic reproach.
“Don’t worry, I’ll save him for you!” Katya whispered rapidly, and she ran out of the room.
“She begged you to forgive her herself, and you could still refuse?” Mitya exclaimed bitterly once more.
“Mitya, don’t you dare blame her; you have no right to!” Alyosha cried hotly.
“It was her proud lips that spoke, not her heart,” Grushenka said in disgust. “If she saves you I’ll forgive her everything—”
She broke off, as though holding something back. She could not yet pull herself together. She had come in, as emerged afterwards, by chance, with no idea of what she would find.
“Alyosha, go after her!” Mitya cried to his brother. “Tell her ... I don’t know what ... just don’t let her leave like this!”

“I’ll come to you again at nightfall,” said Alyosha, and he ran after Katya. He caught up with her outside the hospital grounds. She was walking fast, but as soon as Alyosha reached her she said quickly:

“No, in front of that woman I can’t punish myself! I asked her forgiveness because I wanted to punish myself to the bitter end. She wouldn’t forgive me.... I like her for that!” she added in an unnatural voice, and her eyes flashed with fierce resentment.
“My brother didn’t expect this at all,” muttered Alyosha. “He was sure she wouldn’t come—”

“No doubt. Let’s leave that,” she snapped. “Listen: I can’t go to the funeral with you now. I’ve sent them flowers. I think they still have some money. If they need anything, tell them I’ll never abandon them.... Now go, please, leave me. You’re late already—the bells are ringing for the service.... Please, leave me!”
